label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
**4 out of 5 stars. Worth it for us, with some honest caveats.**

I'm a Lutheran pastor in Minneapolis, not an engineer, so take the technical parts with that in mind. I've learned more about this camera than I expected to, and I'm writing this mainly for other small congregations trying to decide whether to spend money they don't have.

**What we bought and why**

We'd been livestreaming worship on a webcam since 2020. In February 2026 we bought the Lindqvist Optics PT-20 from Chancel AV for $2,140, plus $95 for the wall mount. It has 20x optical zoom, 1080p at 60 frames, and both NDI HX and plain HDMI out. It's powered over the network cable (PoE), so we ran a single cable up to the balcony, which mattered a great deal to us. It feeds OBS on our old office PC and streams to our YouTube channel. Most Sundays we have 30 to 60 people watching.

**Setup**

Our nave is 92 feet long, and the camera sits on the balcony rail at the back. We stored nine presets: altar, pulpit, lectern, font, choir loft, piano, a wide shot, and two for the chancel steps. Twenty times zoom is plenty for that distance. From the back of the balcony we get a tight, clean shot of the pulpit.

The first Sunday wasn't perfect. By the sermon, the presets had drifted a few degrees, enough that the pulpit shot was noticeably off. Firmware update 2.4 came out in March and fixed it, and we haven't had the problem since. If you buy one, update the firmware before you rely on your presets.

The manual is thin and badly translated. I couldn't have figured out some things from it alone. Chancel AV's tech support made up for that. Marcy walked me through things on the phone with real patience and never made me feel foolish for not knowing the vocabulary. That's worth something when you're the pastor and also, apparently, the AV department.

**Running it**

Erik, our 16-year-old acolyte, runs the camera from the free web app on a tablet. He learned it in one afternoon. If your volunteers are teenagers or retirees, the controls won't be what stops you.

One quirk: the autofocus hunts when someone walks between the camera and the pulpit. An usher or a processional cross going by would set it searching. We solved it by locking focus on each preset, and that's worked well. I'd suggest doing that from the start.

**Picture quality**

This is where it earned its price for us. The best review I can offer came from Delores, who is 82 and homebound. She called to tell me she could finally read the hymn numbers on the board. For four years she hadn't been able to.

Low light was the other test. At the Easter Vigil in April, we sang the first "Christ the Lord Is Risen Today" by candlelight only. The picture got grainy, but it stayed usable. You could see people, faces, the candles. The old webcam would have shown nothing but dots, and in past years it did. If your church does candlelight services, this matters.

**What it didn't fix**

The camera does nothing for your sound. Audio isn't its job, and our sound problem is exactly as bad as it was before. I mention this because I suspect some congregations, like ours, think "the stream looks bad" when the bigger complaint is really "the stream sounds bad." If people at home are struggling to hear the sermon, a better camera won't help. Figure out which problem you actually have before you spend.

**Is it worth it?**

For us, yes. I'd buy it again. We have a long nave, a balcony mount, homebound members who rely on the stream, and enough distance that the zoom gets real use.

I'll say plainly that a congregation under 100, or one with a smaller room where the camera can sit closer to the chancel, might do fine with something cheaper. You may not need 20x zoom or nine presets. Think about your room, your distance and your lighting before deciding this is the camera you need.

I took one star off for the preset drift out of the box, the autofocus hunting and the poor manual. The firmware fix and good phone support covered most of that, but you should know going in.

— A Lutheran pastor, Minneapolis
